facts.name: 30-unit program
facts.detail: The prospective-students page describes a 30-unit (10-course) M.S., with 5 required courses, 4 electives, and a capstone.
facts.quote: The M.S. Computer Science degree program is 30 units equivalent to 10 courses. Of these, 5 courses (15 units) are required by all students in the program, 4 courses (12 units) are elective courses, and once course is a capstone experience (3-6 units).

facts.name: Three concentrations
facts.detail: Applicants select a concentration: Computer Science, Computer Networking, or Artificial Intelligence and Machine Learning.
facts.quote: When you apply you will be asked to select a concentration. We currently have three concentrations that allow specialization in a particular area.

facts.name: Typical load
facts.detail: Enrolled M.S. students typically take 1-4 courses (3-12 units) each semester.
facts.quote: Students enrolled in the M.S. graduate program typically take 1-4 courses (3-12 units) each semester, depending on their situation.

facts.name: Admissions review path
facts.detail: Applications go first to the university Office of Admissions and are then forwarded to the Computer Science department for an admit or reject decision.
facts.quote: After the Office of Admissions has completed their review, applications are forwarded to the Computer Science department which makes the decision whether to accept or reject the applicant.

facts.name: GRE required on start page
facts.detail: The assigned start page still says GRE general test scores are required, with preferred percentiles above the 20th verbal and 60th quantitative.
facts.quote: GRE general test scores are required.

facts.name: GRE no longer required on prospective page
facts.detail: The department prospective-students page says GRE scores are no longer required.
facts.quote: Please note: GRE scores are no longer required.
facts.rejectedReason: Rejected by the user: GRE is required. This prospective-students page fact ('GRE scores are no longer required') was not kept.

facts.name: Undergraduate GPA 3.0
facts.detail: Applicants normally need an undergraduate CS or related degree, a 3.0 GPA in all undergraduate work, and a B or better in listed CS and math courses.
facts.quote: must have a grade point average of 3.0 in all undergraduate work, and must have earned a "B" or better in the Computer Science and Mathematics courses listed below.

facts.name: Preferred B+ in important courses
facts.detail: The start page says the department prefers at least a B+ average in the important courses.
facts.quote: Currently, to be eligible for admission into the M.S. program, we prefer at least a B+ average in the important courses.

facts.name: International class standing
facts.detail: For international applicants, the department looks for students who graduated first class or first class with distinction.
facts.quote: For international applicants, we look for students who have graduated first class or first class with distinction.

facts.name: Conditional admission
facts.detail: Applicants missing some course prerequisites may be admitted as Conditionally Classified if they have completed at least Data Structures and most lower-division prerequisites.
facts.quote: may be admitted to the program at the discretion of the department as a "Conditionally Classified Graduate" student, provided the student's record clearly demonstrates the capability of completing all the course requirements after admission.

facts.name: Deficiency grades on start page
facts.detail: The start page says course deficiencies or remediation must be completed with grades of B or better before enrolling in graduate CS courses, and those courses do not count toward the master's degree.
facts.quote: Students must complete any course deficiencies or remediation with grades of "B" or better. Course deficiencies or remediation must be completed before enrolling in graduate Computer Science courses.

facts.name: Prerequisite grade on first-year page
facts.detail: The first-year master's page says each prerequisite must be passed with a B- or better and does not count toward the M.S. degree.
facts.quote: Each prerequisite must be passed with a B− or better and does not count toward the MS degree.

facts.name: Most students conditionally classified
facts.detail: The first-year page says nearly all incoming students are admitted as Conditionally Classified.
facts.quote: Nearly all incoming students are admitted as Conditionally Classified, which means your admission letter lists prerequisite or remediation courses to complete in addition to your graduate coursework.

facts.name: Lower-division CS prerequisites
facts.detail: Required lower-division equivalents include CS 101, CS 201, CS 211, and CS 221.
facts.quote: CS 101 Computer Science I

facts.name: Upper-division CS prerequisites
facts.detail: Required upper-division equivalents include CS 301, CS 311, CS 321, CS 411, CS 413, and CS 421.
facts.quote: CS 301 Data Structures and Algorithms

facts.name: Math prerequisites
facts.detail: Mathematics admission requirements include MATH 130, MATH 131, MATH 225, and STAT 316.
facts.quote: MATH 130 Calculus I

facts.name: Junior college limit
facts.detail: Junior-college courses may fulfill lower-division but not upper-division admission prerequisites.
facts.quote: Courses from junior colleges can be used to fulfill lower division admission prerequisites (100 and 200 level) but not upper division admission prerequisites (300 or 400 level.)

facts.name: Open University note
facts.detail: Students who lack enough prerequisites may use Open University; the page says Open University students have last registration priority and no student visa is sponsored by that program.
facts.quote: While Open University allows students to take courses before being accepted to the Master's program, Open University students have the last registration priority and no student visa are sponsored by the Open University program.

facts.name: Graduate GPA
facts.detail: The first-year page requires 30 units of 600-level coursework, each passed with a C or better, and an overall 3.0 graduate GPA.
facts.quote: The MS in Computer Science requires 30 units of 600-level coursework, each passed with a C or better and an overall 3.0 graduate GPA.

facts.name: Five required core courses
facts.detail: Every student completes five required core courses: CS 601, CS 611, CS 621, CS 651, and CS 671.
facts.quote: Every student completes five required core courses: CS 601, CS 611, CS 621, CS 651, and CS 671.

facts.name: Capstone options
facts.detail: The capstone is the Comprehensive Exam (CS 692), a Project (CS 693), or a Thesis (CS 699).
facts.quote: You also complete a concentration and a capstone — the Comprehensive Exam (CS 692), a Project (CS 693), or a Thesis (CS 699).

facts.name: CS 601
facts.detail: CS 601 Advanced Algorithms (3 units), CSUEB CS department course list: Design, analysis, and implementation of algorithms; asymptotic notation and efficiency classes; recurrence relations; advanced searching and sorting techniques; string matching; heaps and priority queues; linked structures; balanced and threaded trees; graph algorithms; heuristics;
facts.quote: Design, analysis, and implementation of algorithms; asymptotic notation and efficiency classes; recurrence relations; advanced searching and sorting techniques; string matching; heaps and priority queues; linked structures; balanced and threaded trees; graph algorithms; heuristics;

facts.name: CS 621
facts.detail: CS 621 Operating Systems Design (3 units), CSUEB CS department course list: Advanced concepts in operating systems theory and practice. Topics may include process synchronization, concurrency, resource management, security, performance evaluation, analytic models, human interfaces, and implementation issues.
facts.quote: Advanced concepts in operating systems theory and practice. Topics may include process synchronization, concurrency, resource management, security, performance evaluation, analytic models, human interfaces, and implementation issues.

facts.name: CS 651
facts.detail: CS 651 Web Systems (3 units), CSUEB CS department course list: Current practices and trends in software design, development, and deployment of web-based systems, with particular emphasis on e-commerce. Projects incorporating the latest technologies and techniques used by the Internet community. Review of literature.
facts.quote: Current practices and trends in software design, development, and deployment of web-based systems, with particular emphasis on e-commerce. Projects incorporating the latest technologies and techniques used by the Internet community. Review of literature.

facts.name: CS 611
facts.detail: CS 611 Theory of Computation (3 units), CSUEB CS department course list: Alphabets, strings and languages, regular languages and finite automata, context-free languages, grammars, context-sensitivity, Turing machines and Turing-Completeness, decidability, Church-Turing thesis, reducibility, time and space complexity classes, P versus NP, NP-Completeness and NP-Hard
facts.quote: Alphabets, strings and languages, regular languages and finite automata, context-free languages, grammars, context-sensitivity, Turing machines and Turing-Completeness, decidability, Church-Turing thesis, reducibility, time and space complexity classes, P versus NP, NP-Completeness and NP-Hard

facts.name: CS 671
facts.detail: CS 671 Cybersecurity (3 units), CSUEB CS department course list: Security principles, scope and vulnerabilities of Cyberspace, the problem of identity, privacy, malicious software, data security, cryptography, authentication in distributed systems, e-mail security, network security, wireless security, offensive security.
facts.quote: Security principles, scope and vulnerabilities of Cyberspace, the problem of identity, privacy, malicious software, data security, cryptography, authentication in distributed systems, e-mail security, network security, wireless security, offensive security.

facts.name: AI/ML concentration courses
facts.detail: The AI/ML roadmap adds CS 661 Advanced Artificial Intelligence, CS 667 Machine Learning, and CS 663 Computer Vision. The form is dated July 31, 2015.
facts.quote: CS 661      Advanced Artificial Intelligence

facts.name: CS 692
facts.detail: CS 692 Capstone Examinations (3 units), CSUEB CS department course list: A synthesis of important areas of Computer Science, culminating in comprehensive examinations covering three required courses in the Master's degree: Advanced Algorithms, Theory of Computation, and Operating System Design.
facts.quote: A synthesis of important areas of Computer Science, culminating in comprehensive examinations covering three required courses in the Master's degree: Advanced Algorithms, Theory of Computation, and Operating System Design.

facts.name: CS 692 attempts
facts.detail: CS 692 is 3 units, graded CR/NC; students must pass all three exams and have a maximum of three attempts.
facts.quote: CS 692 Capstone Exams is a three (3) unit class. Grading is CR/NC. Students need to pass all three exams to earn a credit for the class.

facts.name: CS 693
facts.detail: CS 693 Capstone Project (1-4 units), CSUEB CS department course list: Implementation of a substantial project in an advanced area of computer science. Supervision by a departmental committee, at least one of whom must be a California State University East Bay Computer Science faculty member.
facts.quote: Implementation of a substantial project in an advanced area of computer science. Supervision by a departmental committee, at least one of whom must be a California State University East Bay Computer Science faculty member.

facts.name: CS 699
facts.detail: CS 699 Capstone Thesis (1-6 units), CSUEB CS department course list: Development and completion of a formal research paper in an advanced area of computer science for submission to the department, which specifies its format. Supervision by a departmental committee, at least one of whom must be a California State University East Bay Computer Science faculty member.
facts.quote: Development and completion of a formal research paper in an advanced area of computer science for submission to the department, which specifies its format. Supervision by a departmental committee, at least one of whom must be a California State University East Bay Computer Science faculty member.

facts.name: Pay fees by the deadline
facts.detail: The first-year page warns students to pay fees by the deadline, even if waitlisted, or they can be dropped from all classes.
facts.quote: Pay your fees by the deadline — even if you are waitlisted. Unpaid fees can drop you from all classes.

facts.name: International full-time enrollment
facts.detail: F-1 students must enroll in at least 8 units each fall and spring and may take only one fully online course per semester.
facts.quote: International (F-1) students must enroll in at least 8 units each fall and spring.

facts.name: Financial aid and prerequisites
facts.detail: Financial aid is based on degree-applicable 600-level units; prerequisites alone do not establish aid eligibility. The page advises including at least 4 units of 600-level coursework each term.
facts.quote: Because prerequisites are undergraduate courses that do not count toward the degree, enrolling in prerequisites alone — even a full load — does not establish aid eligibility.

facts.quote: Advanced concepts of object-oriented design; software development life-cycle models; software modeling; requirements gathering and analysis; pattern-based design of software; patterns as re-usable architecture; implementation of layered architecture code; software testing.

facts.name: CS 605
facts.detail: CS 605 Information Coding and Cryptography (3 units), CSUEB CS department course list: The study of data coding and cryptography. Topics may include: information content, Markov models, data compression codes, error correction and detection codes, symmetric and asymmetric key exchange, and other cryptographic techniques. Programming assignments and review of literature.
facts.quote: The study of data coding and cryptography. Topics may include: information content, Markov models, data compression codes, error correction and detection codes, symmetric and asymmetric key exchange, and other cryptographic techniques. Programming assignments and review of literature.

facts.name: CS 607
facts.detail: CS 607 Parallel Programming (3 units), CSUEB CS department course list: Parallel programming fundamental principles and programming techniques. Topics may include: parallel architectures, principles of parallel algorithm design, programming shared-address space systems and scalable systems, non-numerical and numerical algorithms, GPU Programming, Visualization tools.

Topics may include: parallel architectures, principles of parallel algorithm design, programming shared-address space systems and scalable systems, non-numerical and numerical algorithms, GPU Programming, Visualization tools.

facts.name: CS 615
facts.detail: CS 615 Compiler Design (3 units), CSUEB CS department course list: Overview of compilation, lexical analysis, regular expressions, context-free grammars, top-down parsing and bottom-up parsing, semantic analysis, attribute grammars, ASTs, type-checking, intermediate representations, and constructing simple compilers.
facts.quote: Overview of compilation, lexical analysis, regular expressions, context-free grammars, top-down parsing and bottom-up parsing, semantic analysis, attribute grammars, ASTs, type-checking, intermediate representations, and constructing simple compilers.

facts.detail: CS 623 Cloud Computing (3 units), CSUEB CS department course list: Cloud computing theory and protocols. Topics may include: Infrastructure/Platform/Software - as-a-service, cloud OS, architectures including Federated Clouds, principles of Virtualization platforms, security / privacy issues, Internet of things / data-intensive computing.
facts.quote: Cloud computing theory and protocols. Topics may include: Infrastructure/Platform/Software - as-a-service, cloud OS, architectures including Federated Clouds, principles of Virtualization platforms, security / privacy issues, Internet of things / data-intensive computing.

facts.name: CS 625
facts.detail: CS 625 Advanced Computer Architecture (3 units), CSUEB CS department course list: Analysis and design of computer architecture. facts.quote: Analysis and design of computer architecture. Topics may include: Processor: instruction set principles, building data path, Instruction Pipelining: data/control hazards, Memory Hierarchy: caches, virtual memory, data/thread-level parallelism, multicore and distributed processors.

facts.name: CS 631
facts.detail: CS 631 Database Systems (3 units), CSUEB CS department course list: Design issues in current database systems. Topics may include: data models, storage management and access, distributed systems, query languages and query optimization, database integrity and security, encryption and decryption, concurrency control. Programming projects and review of literature.
facts.quote: Design issues in current database systems. Topics may include: data models, storage management and access, distributed systems, query languages and query optimization, database integrity and security, encryption and decryption, concurrency control. facts.name: CS 641
facts.detail: CS 641 Advanced Computer Networks (3 units), CSUEB CS department course list: Advanced concepts in computer network theory and practice. Specific emphasis on protocols, services, design issues and performance. Topics may include routing, software-defined networks, data-centers, overlay networks, and wireless technologies.
facts.quote: Advanced concepts in computer network theory and practice. Specific emphasis on protocols, services, design issues and performance. Topics may include routing, software-defined networks, data-centers, overlay networks, and wireless technologies.

facts.name: CS 643
facts.detail: CS 643 Distributed Systems (3 units), CSUEB CS department course list: Distributed Systems theory and semantics. Topics may include: temporal logic, proof of program properties, time (logical clocks), state (distributed snapshots), fault-tolerance, replication, rollback recovery, processes and threads, Remote Procedure Calls, file systems.
facts.quote: Distributed Systems theory and semantics. Topics may include: temporal logic, proof of program properties, time (logical clocks), state (distributed snapshots), fault-tolerance, replication, rollback recovery, processes and threads, Remote Procedure Calls, file systems.

facts.quote: Intelligence, rational agent design, state-spaces, search, heuristic functions and A*, game playing, knowledge representation, formal logic, reasoning, expert systems, machine learning paradigms including neural networks and genetic algorithms, introduction to Lisp and Scheme.

facts.quote: Mathematical and algorithmic approaches to the problem of computing properties of the 3-D world from one or more digital images. Topics may include imaging, image processing, feature detection, calibration, stereopsis, motion, object recognition, tracking.

facts.quote: Introduction to machine learning with an emphasis on the underlying mathematics. Topics such as VC dimension, central limit theorem, gradient descent. Applications such as SVM and neural nets.

facts.quote: Digital Signal Processing techniques and applications. Topics may include: Discrete Time Signals and Systems, Discrete Time Networks, Input-Output Relationships, Discrete Time Fourier Transform, Discrete Fourier Transform, IIR and FIR filter design, Power Spectrum Computation.

facts.quote: Introduction to construction and analysis of models by computer simulation. Study of discrete and/or continuous simulation languages. Applications to modeling technological, biological, industrial, and physical processes. Programming projects and review of literature.
